blocks.value:
# One command, four programs

When you run gcc ola.c -o ola, it looks like a single program does everything. Underneath, gcc is a conductor calling four tools in sequence: the preprocessor, the compiler proper, the assembler, and the linker. Each consumes the previous one's product and delivers something new, like stations on an assembly line.

The preprocessor takes your .c, resolves #include and #define, and delivers a translation unit: pure C code with no directives. The compiler translates that C into assembly, the text with your CPU's instructions. The assembler converts the assembly into an object file, the .o, which is already machine code but full of holes: addresses that do not exist yet. The linker closes those holes by joining your objects with the libraries and produces the executable.

The good news is you can stop the line at any station. The -E flag stops after the preprocessor, -S after the compiler and lets you read the assembly, -c after the assembler and saves the .o. With no flags at all, gcc goes to the end and calls the linker.

[["Phase","Consumes","Produces","Flag to stop there"],["Preprocessor",".c source with directives","Expanded C (the translation unit)","-E"],["Compiler","Expanded C","assembly .s","-S"],["Assembler","assembly .s","object .o","-c"],["Linker","objects .o and libraries","executable","none (end of the line)"]]

gcc -E ola.c -o ola.i    # preprocessor: expanded C
gcc -S ola.i -o ola.s    # compiler: readable assembly
gcc -c ola.s -o ola.o    # assembler: binary object
gcc ola.o -o ola         # linker: final executable

# The everyday shortcut fires all four phases at once:
gcc ola.c -o ola

## Why decomposing matters

Knowing which phase you are in changes the diagnosis. An error about a file not found in an #include was born in the preprocessor. A message like error: expected ';' before 'return' is the compiler complaining about syntax. undefined reference to 'soma' is not even the compiler's: it is the linker reporting that someone promised a function no object delivered. Whoever does not know the phases reads everything as a generic compilation error and looks for the cause in the wrong place.

The decomposition is also the key to large builds. Real projects compile each file with -c, often in parallel, and only at the end call the linker once to join the objects. That is what make automates, as you will see in module 5: recompile only the .o whose source changed and redo the link, instead of rebuilding the world on every change.

Keep the vocabulary, because it returns through the whole trail: the preprocessor expands text, the compiler translates to assembly, the assembler produces the object, the linker joins everything. In the coming modules we will open each of these boxes, and this map says where each concept lives.
Saying it gave a compilation error is a lazy diagnosis: the professional first asks which of the four phases complained, because each exposes a different type of problem.

# Scissors and glue before the compiler

The preprocessor does not know C. It sees text and directives starting with #, and works like scissors and glue: #include "mat.h" is literally replaced by the contents of the mat.h file, line by line. That is why a header with a syntax error explodes inside the .c that included it: after the pasting, the compiler sees a single continuous file.

#define creates macros, pure text substitution. #define PI 3.14159 swaps every PI for the number before the compiler wakes up. Macros with parameters look like functions, but are not: #define DOBRO(x) x * 2 applied to DOBRO(1 + 2) expands to 1 + 2 * 2, which equals 5, not 6, because multiplication has precedence. The classic defense is parenthesizing everything: ((x) * 2). A macro with side effects is even worse: MAX(a++, b) may increment a twice, because the argument gets pasted twice in the expanded text.

Conditional directives like #ifdef and #if compile excerpts only on certain platforms or configurations, and are the mechanism behind include guards.

[["Directive","What it does","Typical risk"],["#include","pastes the whole file at that point","double inclusion without a guard"],["#define constant","text swap before compiling","vanishes from types and the debugger"],["#define with parameters","macro mimicking a function","precedence and side effects"],["#ifdef / #if","compiles the excerpt conditionally","untested variants"],["#pragma once","automatic file guard","outside the formal standard, though universal"]]

## Guards, pragma once, and what C++20 changes

Without protection, a header included twice in the same translation unit gets pasted twice, and the duplicate definitions become an error. The include guard solves it with #ifndef MAT_H followed by #define MAT_H: on the second paste the symbol already exists and the whole content is skipped. #pragma once does the same in one line; it is not in the language standard, but in 2026 GCC, Clang, and MSVC support it without drama, and many codebases adopt it.

Pasting has a cost you pay in build time: every .cpp including a huge header recompiles that whole text. C++20 modules attack exactly this: import mat; does not paste text, it imports an interface already compiled once. In 2026 support in GCC, Clang, and build systems is still uneven, so headers still dominate real projects, but that is the direction.

A practical rule to close: prefer const or constexpr constants and inline functions over macros; leave the preprocessor for guards and platform-conditional compilation.
A macro is not a function: it is text pasted in a hurry. Every ten characters it saves gets charged back later in parentheses, duplicated side effects, and hours of debugging.

# What the compiler sees each time

The compiler does not see your project. It sees one translation unit at a time: a .c or .cpp with all the headers already pasted by the preprocessor. While compiling main.cpp, it does not know what exists in mat.cpp; everything it knows about the rest of the world is the declarations the headers brought. This tunnel vision is what allows compiling files in parallel, and it is also the origin of a whole family of errors.

Hence the sacred difference between declaring and defining. Declaring introduces a name and its type: int soma(int, int); says that soma exists somewhere. Defining creates the thing for real: the function's body, the variable's storage. You may declare the same name as many times as you like, in as many units as you like; defining, no.

The one definition rule, ODR, formalizes this: every function or variable used needs exactly one definition in the whole program. Zero definitions give undefined reference at link. Two definitions give multiple definition, also at link.

[["Construct","Declaration or definition?","May repeat across units?"],["int soma(int, int);","declaration","yes, freely"],["int soma(int a, int b) { return a + b; }","definition","no, one per program"],["extern int contador;","declaration","yes, freely"],["int contador = 0;","definition","no, one per program"],["inline int quadrado(int x) { return x * x; }","inline definition","yes, if identical in all"]]

## The role of inline

Modern inline has little to do with speeding up calls: it is an ODR license. Marking a function inline authorizes the same definition to appear in several translation units, as long as identical in all, and the linker is charged with keeping only one. That is why functions defined inside headers must be inline (or live inside a class, which grants implicit inline): without the license, every .cpp including the header would create a definition, and the link would break with multiple definition.

Since C++17 there are also inline variables, finally allowing global constants to be defined in the header without hacks. Another route is static, which gives internal linkage: each unit gets its own private copy invisible to the rest, no conflict, but real duplication.

And if you violate the ODR with different definitions across units, a quadrado(x) that adds in one file and multiplies in another? The linker is not required to notice: it may silently pick one version. The standard classifies this as an ill-formed program with no required diagnostic, in practice undefined behavior.
Declaring is promising, defining is delivering. The compiler accepts promises all day; the linker is the collector demanding exactly one delivery per name.

# The .o inside: code and promises

An object file is not just machine code. It is a container (on Linux, in ELF format) with separate sections: .text holds the instructions, .data holds initialized global variables, .bss notes the zeroed ones. And, alongside them, two structures that matter a lot: the symbol table and the relocation entries.

The symbol table is the list of what that object defines and what it consumes. When main.c calls soma and printf, main.o records: I define main; I need soma and printf, which I do not know where live. Defined symbols have an address inside the object; undefined ones are promises the linker will have to fulfill with other objects or libraries.

The tool for seeing this is nm. Running nm main.o lists each symbol with a letter: T for code defined in .text, U for undefined, D for initialized data, B for zeroed data. nm turns the .o from a black box into a readable inventory, and it will be your magnifying glass in module 4 and the final project.

$ gcc -c main.c
$ nm main.o
0000000000000000 T main
                 U printf
                 U soma

$ gcc -c mat.c && nm mat.o
0000000000000000 T soma

# After the link, the promise becomes an address:
$ gcc main.o mat.o -o app && nm app | grep -E "main|soma"
0000000000001139 T main
0000000000001160 T soma

[["Letter in nm","Meaning","Typical example"],["T","defined in the code section (.text)","a global function of the file"],["t","code with internal linkage","a static function of the file"],["U","undefined: used, defined elsewhere","printf called in main.o"],["D","initialized global data (.data)","int limite = 100;"],["B","zeroed global data (.bss)","int total; with no initial value"]]

## Relocation: the holes the linker fills

When the assembler generates the instruction calling soma, it cannot know the function's final address, which may not even exist yet. So it records a placeholder in the address's place and creates a relocation entry: a note saying that at that offset in .text there is a pending call to the symbol soma. The object is full of these notes, one per external reference.

At link time, the linker joins all the objects' sections, decides each symbol's address, and goes around paying the notes: where there was a hole, the real address goes in. That is why a .o does not run alone: it is a puzzle with missing pieces, playable only after the linker fits everything together.

This mechanism explains the U in nm concretely. U is not an error or a warning: it is the natural state of an object depending on others. It only becomes a problem if, at link time, no object or library offers the promised symbol, and then you meet again the undefined reference from the first lesson.
An object file is a half-signed contract: it signs what it delivers, lists what it expects to receive. nm is the fastest way to read that contract before the linker comes to collect.

# Two ways of borrowing code

Almost no program lives on its own objects alone: it borrows code from libraries, and there are two forms of borrowing. The static library, the .a, is a package of .o files created by ar. At link, the needed objects are copied into your executable, and the debt is settled there: the binary becomes self-sufficient, never needing the .a file again.

The dynamic library, the .so (shared object), stays outside the binary. The link only records the dependency, and what truly resolves it is the dynamic loader, at run time: it locates the .so, maps it into memory, and connects the symbols. The ldd command shows this dependency list, and it is the first step in investigating any library problem.

The choice is a classic trade-off. Static gives a bigger binary, but portable and predictable: what you tested is what runs. Dynamic gives a smaller binary, memory shared between processes, and centralized updates, at the cost of depending on the environment where the program will run.

[["Criterion","Static (.a)","Dynamic (.so)"],["When the code enters","at link, copied into the binary","at run, by the loader"],["Executable size","bigger","smaller"],["Security patch on the lib","recompile and reinstall each binary","swapping the .so fixes all at once"],["Deploy dependency","none, self-sufficient binary","the right .so must exist on the machine"],["Memory across processes","each with its own copy","code shared among them"]]

# Static: package objects and copy at link
ar rcs libmat.a mat.o
gcc main.o -L. -lmat -o app_estatico

# Dynamic: position-independent code, separate .so
gcc -fPIC -shared mat.c -o libmat.so
gcc main.o -L. -lmat -o app_dinamico

$ ./app_dinamico
./app_dinamico: error while loading shared libraries:
libmat.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file...

$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./app_dinamico   # loader finds the lib
42

## The famous error and where the loader looks

The error in the example above is an absolute classic: the binary linked perfectly, but at run time the loader did not find libmat.so. Note the moment: it is not a compilation error nor a link error, it is a load error. The loader searches standard directories like /lib and /usr/lib, the cache maintained by ldconfig, and the paths recorded in the binary itself via rpath or runpath.

LD_LIBRARY_PATH is the environment variable adding directories to this search, ahead of the rest. It is great for testing a freshly compiled library without installing anything, and terrible as a permanent solution: a forgotten export in your profile changes which .so every program loads, creating bugs that only exist on your machine. For distribution, the professional path is installing the lib in a system directory and running ldconfig, or recording an rpath at link.

Dynamic linking's decisive argument shows up in security: when a patch comes out for a library like OpenSSL, updating the system .so fixes every program using it, without recompiling any. With static linking, each binary embeds its copy and must be rebuilt and redistributed one by one.
Static linking freezes the dependency inside the binary; dynamic bets on the environment. Both charge: one in size and redistribution, the other in works-on-my-machine bugs.

# The first reading of your code

To the compiler, your file is just a row of characters: i, n, t, space, x. The front end's first step is the lexer (lexical analyzer), which walks that row and groups it into tokens: the smallest units with meaning. int becomes a keyword token, x becomes an identifier, = becomes an operator, 42 becomes a numeric literal, ; becomes punctuation. Spaces and comments are consumed and thrown away: they separate tokens but do not become tokens.

Each token carries its category and its lexeme, the original text. That is an important distinction: the lexer does not know what x means, whether it was declared, whether the type matches. It only knows x looks like an identifier. Interpreting relationships between tokens is the job of the following phases.

How does the lexer decide where a token ends? By the maximal munch rule: it eats the longest stretch that still forms a valid token. That is why a>>b reads >> as a single shift operator, not as two greater-than signs in a row.

int media = (a + b) / 2;

/* The lexer sees the line above like this:
   [keyword: int] [identifier: media] [operator: =]
   [punctuation: (] [identifier: a] [operator: +]
   [identifier: b] [punctuation: )] [operator: /]
   [literal: 2] [punctuation: ;]                        */

int 2x = 10;   /* error: invalid suffix "x" on integer
                  constant: the lexer choked on 2x    */

[["Token category","Examples","How the lexer recognizes it"],["Keyword","int, while, return","identifier present in the reserved list"],["Identifier","media, contador, x2","letter or _ followed by letters, digits, _"],["Literal","42, 3.14, 'a', \"oi\"","digits, quotes, and valid numeric forms"],["Operator","+, *, >>, ==","symbols, always maximal munch"],["Punctuation","; , ( ) { }","isolated structural characters"]]

## Keywords, identifiers, and the lexical error

Keyword and identifier look the same: letters. The difference is a closed list: after recognizing a name, the lexer consults the language's reserved-word table; if the lexeme is there, the token is a keyword, otherwise an identifier. That is exactly why int int = 3; makes no sense to the compiler and why you cannot name a variable while.

A lexical error is when the row of characters does not even form valid tokens. Real examples: a character outside the language, like a lone @ in the middle of C code; an open string without the final quote, which gcc reports as missing terminating \" character; or the classic 2x, which gcc rejects with invalid suffix "x" on integer constant, because a number cannot spill into a letter and 2x is not a valid identifier either.

Notice almost everything we call a typo in daily life is not lexical: forgetting a ; produces perfectly valid tokens in invalid order. That is a syntax error, the parser's business, the next lesson.
The lexer is a reader without interpretation: it recognizes the words of the text, but not the grammar of the sentences. It says x is a name; whether the name makes sense is no longer its problem.

lessons.title: Parser and grammar: the tree is born

blocks.value:
# From tokens to structure

The parser (syntax analyzer) receives the token queue and answers one question: does this sequence obey the language's grammar? The grammar is the set of rules defining how valid sentences form: an expression can be a number, or two expressions joined by an operator; an if requires parentheses and a statement. If the tokens fit no rule, out comes the famous error: expected ';' before 'return': a syntax error.

When they fit, the parser produces the AST, the abstract syntax tree. Each internal node is an operation; the leaves are numbers and variables. Abstract because it discards what was mere notation: parentheses, semicolons, and commas do not become nodes, they merely guided the assembly.

The tree is the perfect structure for what comes next: it can be walked, type-checked, optimized, and used to generate code. Text is good for humans; the tree is the format the compiler thinks in. All the magic of the next phases operates on it.

## Precedence and associativity

Consider 2 + 3 * 4. The token queue is flat, but the result must be 14, not 20. What guarantees that is the precedence embedded in the grammar: multiplication binds tighter than addition, so the parser builds the tree with + at the root, holding 2 and the * node, which in turn holds 3 and 4. Evaluation climbs from leaf to root: 3 * 4 first, then 2 + 12. If you write (2 + 3) * 4, the parentheses invert the assembly: * takes the root and the addition drops below it.

Precedence resolves different operators; associativity resolves ties between identical operators. 10 - 4 - 3 could be (10 - 4) - 3 = 3 or 10 - (4 - 3) = 9. Subtraction associates left, so the first tree holds. Assignment associates right: a = b = 5 means a = (b = 5), and that is why chaining works.

Keep the image: precedence decides who stays closer to the leaves; associativity decides which way the tree leans on a tie. Every expression you write becomes exactly one tree, no ambiguity.

The AST is the sentence after being understood: the structure remains, the punctuation falls away. A parenthesis does not become a node; it only decides which tree gets born, and vanishes in the act.

# Correct sentences that make no sense

A sentence can be grammatically perfect and still absurd. The green sleeps quickly passes Portuguese syntax and fails on meaning. Code is the same: x = y + 1; is impeccable syntax, but if y was never declared, or if y is a struct, the sentence has no meaning. Checking meaning is the work of semantic analysis, the front end's third stage, which walks the AST assembled by the parser.

Three checks dominate. Name resolution: every use of an identifier must point to a visible declaration; this is where gcc's error: 'y' undeclared (first use in this function) is born. Scope: the same variable can exist in different blocks, and the analysis decides which declaration holds at each point, always the innermost block's. Type checking: every operation needs compatible operands; adding int with float promotes the int, but adding struct with int earns error: invalid operands to binary +.

This phase's product is an annotated tree: each node gains its type and each name its declaration.

## Syntactic or semantic? The diagnostic reflex

Telling the two error families apart changes your fixing speed. A syntactic error is of form: the tokens do not fit the grammar. The messages talk about expected something before something, and the fix is usually mechanical: a forgotten ;, an extra brace, an unmatched parenthesis. A semantic error is of meaning: the form is right, but a name does not exist, a type does not match, a call has wrong arguments. The messages cite undeclared, invalid operands, incompatible types, and the fix demands thinking: what was the intent?

One detail that confuses beginners: the compiler processes declarations top to bottom within the translation unit. Using a function defined further down in the same file, with no prototype before it, produces a warning or error depending on the mode; that is why headers collect prototypes.

And it is worth repeating the trail's map: none of this is the undefined reference. That one belongs to the linker, a later phase, and speaks of a symbol with no definition in any object. Semantic analysis's undeclared speaks of a name with no visible declaration in the current unit. Similar messages, different phases and fixes.
The parser checks the sentence's form; semantic analysis checks whether the sentence means anything. Expected ';' is form. Undeclared is meaning. Knowing which of the two spoke is half the fix.

# Always the first one

You compile and the screen dumps forty errors. The panic reaction is scrolling to the end and attacking the last one; the professional technique is the opposite: read the first error, fix it, recompile. The reason is the cascade: after a real error, the parser loses the thread and starts interpreting valid tokens from a broken state, manufacturing ghost errors. A forgotten ; in a struct or an unmatched brace at the top of the file produces dozens of complaints on lines that are perfectly fine.

A classic example: forget the ; closing a struct definition in a header. gcc complains in every file including that header, with messages about the first function declared after it, something like expected ';' before or two or more data types in declaration specifiers, pointing at innocent lines. Whoever hunts the forty errors one by one loses the afternoon; whoever fixes the first watches the other thirty-nine evaporate on the next recompile.

Read the whole message, with file and line, and also look at the line BEFORE the one pointed to: punctuation errors usually live just above where they are perceived.

Errors involving STL templates scare by volume: g++ prints the whole instantiation stack, with kilometer-long type names, and ninety percent of the lines cite system headers you never opened. Second, extract the final verdict, which is usually short: no match for 'operator<', or no matching function for call. # The mental mini interpreter

You already know every expression becomes a tree. Now comes the exercise that welds that knowledge: evaluating the tree in your head, like an interpreter would. The rule is a single one, called the post-order walk: to know a node's value, first resolve the left child, then the right, and only then apply the node's operator. Leaves are trivial: a number is worth itself; a variable is worth whatever memory says.

Take (8 - 3) * (4 + 2 * 5) - 1. The root is the last - (left associativity). Before subtracting, I need the left side: the *. Before the *, its two children: 8 - 3 = 5 and, on the other branch, 4 + 2 * 5, whose internal tree puts the * below: 2 * 5 = 10, then 4 + 10 = 14. Now the upper *: 5 * 14 = 70. Finally the root: 70 - 1 = 69.

Notice what you just did: walked the whole tree without writing anything, always resolving bottom up. That is exactly a expression interpreter's algorithm.

## Why this exercise is worth gold

First, it reveals that interpreting is walking: the heart of an expression interpreter is the few recursive lines in the example, and you just ran them mentally. The recursion mirrors the tree; the base case is the leaf. When the trail discusses optimization in the next module, you will recognize constant folding as exactly this: the compiler evaluating in post-order, at compile time, the branches whose children are constants.

Second, the habit changes how you read hard code. Facing a loaded expression, the amateur reads left to right and gets lost; whoever thinks in trees finds the operator with the LOWEST precedence, which is the root, splits the expression in two halves, and solves each. The right question is never which operation comes first in the line, but who is the root of this subtree.

Train with your own expressions: write one, draw the tree, evaluate in post-order, and check with a printf. Three or four rounds suffice to make it a reflex, and that reflex will be demanded in the module 7 project.

Evaluating in post-order is reading like the machine: children before the parent, leaves before everything. Whoever masters this walk never again argues precedence by guesswork; draws the tree and done.

# Why there is a middle of the road

Between the AST and the assembly, modern compilers insert one more layer: the intermediate representation, or IR. It is an internal language, neither C nor assembly: like an idealized assembly, with infinite registers and simple, regular instructions, without any specific CPU's quirks. The AST becomes IR, the IR is optimized dozens of times, and only at the end does it become the target's assembly.

The most cited reason is engineering arithmetic. Suppose N languages (C, C++, Rust, Swift) and M architectures (x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V). Without an IR, you would need N times M complete translators, each with its own optimizations. With an IR in the middle, N front ends translating language to IR and M back ends translating IR to machine suffice: N plus M pieces, and the optimizations are written ONCE, over the IR, valid for all combinations.

The deeper reason is that the IR is the right format for optimizing: regular enough for automatic analysis, abstract enough not to depend on a CPU.

## LLVM IR, the reference in 2026

The LLVM project turned this architecture into a platform. Clang is a front end translating C and C++ to LLVM IR; Rust and Swift do the same with their own front ends; and all inherit for free the same package: LLVM's optimizer and back ends for x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V, GPUs, and WebAssembly. In 2026, LLVM IR is the market's reference intermediate representation: when someone creates a new language and wants competitive performance, the standard path is emitting LLVM IR and riding the infrastructure.

GCC follows the same philosophy with other acronyms: the front end generates GIMPLE, the form used by high-level optimizations, which later descends to RTL before becoming assembly. The names change, the architecture is the same: front end understands the language, middle end optimizes the IR, back end knows the machine.

For you, the practical consequence is liberating: optimization is not per-language magic. The bulk of what the next chapter shows happens in the IR, and holds equally for C, C++, or Rust compiled by the same infrastructure.
The IR is the compiler's lingua franca: front ends arrive speaking C, C++, or Rust, back ends leave speaking x86 or ARM, and in the middle everyone negotiates in the same language.

# The compiler rewrites your code

Optimizing is rewriting while preserving observable behavior: same result, less work. Four classic transformations set the tone. Constant folding: arithmetic between constants is done at compilation; int s = 60 * 60 * 24; becomes 86400 directly, and the product vanishes from the binary. Constant propagation: if x received 5 and did not change, uses of x become 5, which usually creates new folds in a chain.

Inlining: the call of a small function is replaced by its own body. It removes the call's cost, but the bigger effect is another: with the body exposed in context, the other optimizations see through the border that previously blocked them. Dead code elimination (DCE): code not affecting the observable result is removed, from an if (0) to a variable computed and never read.

The beautiful part is the domino effect: propagation turns variables into constants, folding does the arithmetic, conditions become fixed false and DCE prunes the whole branch. One optimization opens the next one's door.

## The contract: observable behavior

The license for all this is the as-if rule: the compiler may rewrite at will, as long as the program's observable behavior does not change: the outputs, the accesses to volatile variables, the calls to functions whose effect it does not know. Inside this fence, variables vanish, functions disappear, loops change shape.

That explains two common surprises. First: in the debugger, with optimization on, you try to print a variable and get value optimized out; it no longer exists, it became a constant or a register. Second: your naive benchmark clocks zero nanoseconds; the loop that only computed something never read was pruned entirely by DCE, and you measured nothing.

The limit also becomes clear: the compiler only optimizes what it can PROVE. If the variable can be changed by another path, if the called function is opaque, if the pointer can point anywhere, it retreats to the conservative path. Simple, local code is code the optimizer sees; and in the next lesson you control how hard it tries.

The binary is not your code translated; it is your code rewritten by an obsessive reviewer cutting everything that does not change the result. If the variable vanished from the debugger, it probably never needed to exist.

# The compiler's effort dial

Optimizations do not all come on by default: you pick the package with the -O flag. With -O0, the gcc and clang default, the compiler translates almost literally: every variable lives in memory, no inlining, the assembly mirrors the source. It is the fastest mode to compile and the most faithful to debug. -O1 turns on the cheap essentials. -O2 is the complete package of optimizations that do not bet heavily on space: the industry's standard release level, and the one Linux distribution packagers use at scale.

-O3 goes beyond -O2 with more aggressive loop transformations and bolder vectorization, which usually inflates code. Sometimes it truly wins on numeric code; sometimes it ties or even loses to -O2, because bigger code pressures the instruction cache. The honest answer is: measure on YOUR program.

Two letters complete the menu: -Os optimizes like -O2 but prioritizing size, and -Og optimizes without disturbing the debugger. Both have owners, as you will see next.

# The same file, four different contracts:
gcc -O0 -g app.c -o app_debug     # faithful to the source, gdb happy
gcc -O2 app.c -o app_release      # the production standard
gcc -O3 -march=native app.c -o a  # aggressive, only with measurement
gcc -Os app.c -o app_flash        # every byte counts

size app_release app_flash        # compare the .text section
#    text    data     bss     dec
#   14232     616       8   14856  app_release
#    9848     616       8   10472  app_flash

## Os to fit, Og to debug

-Os is the level of embedded systems. On a microcontroller with 128 KB of flash, the -O3 that unrolls loops and inflates code may simply not fit; -Os applies the -O2 playbook while vetoing whatever grows, and still gains performance where smaller code uses the cache better. GCC firmware for ARM is usually born with -Os as a project default, and the ruler is the .text size measured by size on every build.

-Og solves another pain: debugging with -O0 gets slow on large programs, but debugging with -O2 is frustrating, with value optimized out and gdb's cursor jumping lines out of order. -Og turns on the optimizations that do not destroy the correspondence between binary and source. Combine with -g, which emits the debug symbols; and remember -g does not change the generated code, it only attaches information, so -O2 -g is perfectly valid for investigating production.

The closing criterion: -O0 or -Og with -g for developing, -O2 for shipping, -Os when bytes are gold, -O3 only with a benchmark proving the gain.
Going from -O2 to -O3 without measuring is not optimization, it is superstition: sometimes the bigger code loses exactly where you swore it would win.

# The contract you signed without reading

The C and C++ standard defines the language's behavior, but leaves deliberate holes: situations of undefined behavior, UB, about which it promises NOTHING. Signed integer overflow, reading past an array's end, dereferencing a null pointer, using an uninitialized variable: if your program does that, the standard washes its hands, and any result is conforming.

The trick is understanding what the optimizer does with these holes: it assumes UB NEVER happens in your program, and uses that assumption as an axiom in the proofs authorizing optimizations. If x is int, the compiler reasons: x + 1 > x is always true, because if x + 1 overflowed, that would be UB, and UB does not happen. The integer comparison becomes the constant true and vanishes from the binary.

It is not malice: it is the other face of the speed you demand. Without assuming the absence of UB, every addition would need an overflow check and every loop would lose valuable transformations. The license that speeds up correct code is the same one that surprises incorrect code.

## The famous cases and the professional posture

The null check example is real history: in 2009, a Linux kernel driver dereferenced the pointer before testing it; gcc, correctly, deduced the pointer could not be null and removed the test. The missing check became an exploitable vulnerability, and the episode entered every UB talk since. Another classic: loops with an int counter and comparisons the compiler rewrites assuming overflow never comes, breaking code that counted on the wraparound.

The professional posture has three points. First: UB is not an error the compiler detects and punishes; it is a premise it uses silently; the program may even appear to work at -O0 and change its face at -O2, and both are conforming. Second: do not negotiate with UB; write the check BEFORE the use, use unsigned or wider types when overflow is possible. Third: instrument; UBSan, introduced in module 6, catches exactly these traps at runtime.

UB is the price of C and C++ performance. Knowing it is what separates respect from fear.

The optimizer does not hunt undefined behavior to punish you; it proves theorems starting from the axiom that UB does not exist in your code. If the axiom is false, the proof comes out elegant and wrong.

# The window into what the compiler did

Everything this module asserted about optimization is verifiable in seconds, and the tool that made this a worldwide habit is the Compiler Explorer, godbolt.org, created by Matt Godbolt. You paste a function in the left panel, pick compiler and flags, and the assembly appears on the right, colored by source line, updating on every keystroke. In 2026 it carries GCC and Clang in dozens of versions and targets, from x86-64 to ARM and RISC-V, and it is free in the browser.

The fundamental exercise is comparing -O0 with -O2 side by side. At -O0, the function soma_ate(n) becomes dozens of lines: every variable read and written on the stack, the loop faithful to the source. At -O2, the same arithmetic-sum loop usually becomes half a dozen jump-free instructions, because the compiler recognized the closed formula, or a vectorized loop. Seeing that once teaches more than ten articles.

Locally, the equivalent is gcc -S -O2 arquivo.c, which leaves the .s on disk; godbolt just removes the friction until it becomes a reflex.

Make it an engineering routine: before claiming a micro-optimization in the source improves anything, paste both versions into godbolt and compare the assembly at -O2. Most of the time the compiler already did that on its own, and the change only hurt readability. The answer is one tab away, and mature teams in 2026 treat the godbolt link as a standard attachment in performance discussions.

# Why C++ decorates names

In C, the function soma becomes the symbol soma, and that is it. In C++, the same function becomes something like _Z4somaii, and there is a solid reason: overloading. C++ allows several soma functions, one for int and int, another for double and double, and the linker, which only knows names, must distinguish them. The solution is name mangling: the compiler encodes the full signature in the symbol, name, namespace, parameter types. _Z4somaii decomposes into: _Z the scheme's prefix, 4soma the name with its length in front, ii two int parameters.

The scheme is an ABI convention, not part of the language. GCC and Clang on Linux follow the same one, the Itanium C++ ABI, and that is why objects from both link with each other; MSVC on Windows uses another, incompatible one.

To translate back there is c++filt: echo the symbol into it and receive the readable signature. nm accepts the -C flag, which already prints everything demangled. Keep this pair: it turns C++ link errors from hieroglyph into sentence.

$ cat mat.cpp
int soma(int a, int b)       { return a + b; }
double soma(double a, double b) { return a + b; }

$ g++ -c mat.cpp && nm mat.o
0000000000000000 T _Z4somadd
0000000000000024 T _Z4somaii

$ echo _Z4somaii | c++filt
soma(int, int)

$ nm -C mat.o        # -C already applies the demangle
0000000000000000 T soma(double, double)
0000000000000024 T soma(int, int)

## extern "C": the bridge between the two worlds

Mangling creates a classic boundary problem. A library compiled in C exports the raw symbol init_driver; your C++ program includes the header, the compiler decorates the reference to _Z11init_driverv, and the link fails with undefined reference, even with the library right there. The two speak of identical functions with different symbol names.

The bridge is extern "C": it declares that those functions follow the C convention, no mangling. That is why C library headers prepared to coexist with C++ carry the consecrated pattern: an extern "C" { ... } block guarded by #ifdef __cplusplus, so the same header works in both compilers. You see it in practically every system header.

The bridge's cost: extern "C" functions cannot be overloaded, since they would all dispute the same raw symbol. And the diagnostic rule stays: undefined reference with a decorated name while the library's nm shows the clean name (or the reverse) screams mixed conventions; the answer is almost always a missing extern "C" in the header.
The linker does not know what overloading is: it matches strings. Mangling exists to turn C++'s richness of types into distinct strings, and c++filt exists so you can read what the compiler wrote.

# The link's most famous error

undefined reference to 'soma': no toolchain message has been typed into search engines more. The anatomy is simple: some object USES the symbol soma (nm's U), and no object or library in the link command DEFINES it (the T that should exist). Note who speaks: not the compiler, but ld, usually via collect2 in gcc's output. Your code may be perfect; what failed was the puzzle's assembly.

The true causes fit a short list. First, the champion: the object or library defining the symbol stayed out of the command; you compiled main.c and forgot mat.o. Second: the order of arguments; static libraries must come AFTER whoever uses them, as the next lesson unpacks. Third, typical of C++: the signature does not match; you declared soma(int, int) in the header but defined soma(long, long) in the .cpp, and the decorated symbols differ. Fourth: the C++ side forgot the lib was C, the extern "C" case from the last lesson.

With the causes mapped, diagnosis becomes routine, and that is what the next block assembles.

main.cpp:(.text+0x1a): undefined reference to 'soma(int, int)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

# Step 1: who NEEDS the symbol?
$ nm -C main.o | grep soma

# Step 2: who DEFINES the symbol?
$ nm -C mat.o | grep soma
0000000000000000 T soma(long, long)   # found the culprit:
                                      # different signature

## The method: nm on both sides

The professional diagnosis has three steps and fits in a minute. Step one: read the whole error and note the exact symbol, demangled if C++. Step two: confirm who consumes it; nm -C over the object cited in the message must show the symbol with U. Step three: look for who should provide it; run nm -C over each .o and nm -C on the suspect library, filtering with grep. Three possible endings: the symbol appears with T nowhere, so something needs compiling or linking; it appears with T in a file not in the command, so include the file; it appears similar but not identical, so the signature diverged, compare the types carefully.

Two refinements close the lesson. If the T exists in a static library ALREADY in the command, suspect the argument order, the next lesson's topic. And learn the vtable variant: undefined reference to 'vtable for MinhaClasse' indicates a virtual method declared and never defined, a classic of whoever forgot the destructor's body. The message scares; the method solves it the same way.

# Order in the command matters

Here is a behavior that has burned hours of many good people: gcc -lmat main.o fails with undefined reference, while gcc main.o -lmat links cleanly. Same library, same object, only the order changed. The reason is the linker's algorithm with static libraries: it processes arguments LEFT to RIGHT, keeping a list of pending symbols, and from a .a it only pulls the objects resolving pendings existing AT THAT moment.

In the broken command, libmat.a is examined first, when there is no pending anything; nothing gets pulled, and it is dismissed. Then main.o arrives, recording the pending soma, but the library is already behind: the linker does not go back. In the right command, main.o enters first and notes the debt; when libmat.a arrives, the object with soma is pulled and the account closes.

The rule of thumb: objects first, libraries after, and whoever USES comes before whoever PROVIDES. Between libraries the same holds: if liba depends on libb, write -la -lb, in that order.

$ gcc -lmat main.o -o app          # wrong order
/usr/bin/ld: main.o: undefined reference to 'soma'

$ gcc main.o -lmat -L. -o app      # user before provider
$ ./app
42

# Circular dependency between statics: a resolves with b,
# b resolves with a. Either repeat the first at the end...
gcc main.o -la -lb -la -L. -o app
# ...or ask the linker for a group scan:
gcc main.o -Wl,--start-group -la -lb -Wl,--end-group -L. -o app

## Weak symbols: the default that yields

One concept is missing to close the linker's vocabulary: the weak symbol. A normal (strong) symbol fights: two T's for the same name give multiple definition. A symbol marked weak, with the weak attribute of GCC and Clang, offers itself as a polite default: if nobody else defines that name, the weak version holds; if a strong definition appears, it wins without conflict, and the linker does not even complain.

The classic use lives in the embedded world, and you will meet it again: vendors' startup files define each interrupt handler as a weak alias to a default infinite loop. Your firmware defines a strong UART_Handler, and it replaces the default automatically; interrupts you did not handle keep falling into the safe loop. Libraries use the same trick to offer replaceable hooks, like a default malloc a custom allocator can override.

In nm, weak symbols appear as W or w instead of T. It is worth knowing how to read it: an unexpected W explains why your function was silently swapped for another, with no duplicate error along the way.
The static linker reads left to right and never looks back: a library examined before the debt exists is a dismissed library. Objects first, libraries after, dependents before dependencies.

# The memory map has an owner

Until here the linker looked like a joiner of objects, but it has a second, quieter job: deciding the ADDRESS of everything. Someone must determine that .text starts at such point, that .data comes after, that the stack grows from there. That someone is the linker script: a file in ld's language describing the available memories and dispatching each input section to an output region.

On the desktop you never see it because ld uses a built-in default script (print it with ld --verbose), suitable for Linux executables loaded by the operating system with virtual memory. The sections you know from nm are exactly what it organizes: .text with code, .rodata with constants, .data with initialized globals, .bss with the zeroed ones.

The core syntax fits in two blocks: MEMORY declares the regions, with origin and length; SECTIONS maps each section to a region. Reading a script answers three questions: which memories exist, what goes in each, and who copies what at startup.

## Why embedded edits this file

On a microcontroller there is no operating system or loader: the binary is written to real physical addresses, and the chip powers on executing from the flash's reset address. The chip's memory map, how much flash, how much RAM, where each starts, must be written somewhere, and that place is the linker script the vendor ships with the SDK. Switching chips within the same family often boils down to adjusting ORIGIN and LENGTH.

The script also explains an embedded startup ritual: .data needs initial values, but RAM loses power; so the initial image lives in flash (the AT > FLASH in the example) and the startup code copies it to RAM before main, besides zeroing .bss. Without understanding the script, this stretch of startup looks like magic.

And when the code does not fit, the error comes from ld and cites the script: region 'FLASH' overflowed by 1234 bytes. It is the hook for the next lesson: measuring what each section occupies and slimming the binary.

On the desktop, the memory map is inherited and invisible; in embedded, it is a file of yours, with a name, addresses, and size. Whoever never read a linker script still does not know where their own code lives.

# Before cutting, measure

Your C++ hello world has hundreds of KB and your neighbor's in C has tens? Before any opinion, measure. The first ruler is size, which shows the total per section: text (code and constants), data (initialized globals), bss (zeroed ones, which take RAM but no file). The second is the link map: gcc -Wl,-Map=app.map makes the linker write a report of where every symbol of every object landed, with address and size. It is the binary's bank statement: sort by the largest and the source of the bloat appears with first and last name.

For a per-symbol view straight from the binary, nm --size-sort -C lists functions by size order, and tools like bloaty, popular in 2026, aggregate by section, by file, and by template.

Only after measuring comes the scissors. And the first scissors is strip: it removes the symbol table and debug information, which in a binary compiled with -g dominate the file. The code does not change a byte; only what served gdb and nm goes away.

$ g++ -O2 -g app.cpp -o app
$ size app
   text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
  18744    1024     280   20048    4e50 app

$ ls -lh app
-rwxrwxr-x 1 dev dev 342K app     # -g dominates the file

$ strip app && ls -lh app
-rwxrwxr-x 1 dev dev  22K app     # code intact, debug out

# The full statement, symbol by symbol:
$ g++ -O2 app.cpp -Wl,-Map=app.map -o app
$ grep -n "\.text" app.map | head

## What bloats a C++ binary

With the map in hand, C++'s usual suspects get a face. Templates: each type combination instantiates a complete copy of the code; a std::map for five type pairs is five maps in the binary, and the map file shows the giant decorated names repeating. RTTI and exceptions: typeid, dynamic_cast, and stack unwinding carry tables; embedded projects usually compile with -fno-rtti -fno-exceptions, a trade with language consequences, never a universal default.

Two flags make the linker truly prune: -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections at compilation put each function in its own section, and -Wl,--gc-sections at link discards the sections nobody references. In firmware, this pair often cuts tens of percent.

The criterion closes the lesson: on the desktop, KBs rarely justify losing readability; distribute with strip and done. In the embedded world of the previous lesson, every byte disputes flash with features, and the diet is real engineering. Measure with size and map, cut at the right source, and never sacrifice clarity for bytes that make no difference.
A fat binary is not solved with opinion: the map file says exactly which symbols weigh how much. Measure, sort, cut the biggest; repeating the same strip on faith does not slim anyone twice.

# The problem before the tool

Imagine a project with forty .c files. Compiling everything on every change, gcc *.c, works and is a disaster: you edit one line and wait minutes redoing work already done. The manual alternative, remembering which files changed and recompiling only them, breaks at the first detail: a HEADER changed, now what? Every .c including it needs recompiling, and those not including it do not. Keeping this reasoning in your head does not scale; forgetting one file generates the worst bug: the executable assembled from old objects, matching no source at all.

make, created in the 70s and omnipresent to this day, solves it with an elegant idea: you declare the dependency GRAPH, who produces what from what, and it derives the build plan. app depends on main.o and mat.o; main.o depends on main.c and mat.h; mat.o depends on mat.c and mat.h.

With the graph in hand, the rebuild decision uses the file system's timestamps: if any prerequisite is newer than the target, the target is stale and the recipe runs; otherwise, nothing to do.

# Minimal Makefile: the declared graph
app: main.o mat.o
	gcc main.o mat.o -o app

main.o: main.c mat.h
	gcc -c main.c

mat.o: mat.c mat.h
	gcc -c mat.c

# $ make          -> builds what is needed, in the right order
# $ make          -> make: 'app' is up to date.
# $ touch mat.h && make   -> recompiles both .o and relinks

## The contract and the header trap

Notice the contract: make does not understand C, does not read your code, guesses nothing. It compares dates and executes recipes, and the whole intelligence lives in the graph YOU declared. This has a treacherous consequence: if main.c includes mat.h, but main.o's rule does not list mat.h as a prerequisite, make has no way to know. You edit the header, run make, and it answers up to date while the binary runs the old version. That is the classic broken build only make clean cures, and the cause is always the same: a lying graph.

That is why serious projects generate header dependencies automatically: gcc does the job with the -MMD -MP flags, which produce .d files listing every included header, ready for make to import. The modern build systems in the rest of the module do this by default.

The idea of graph plus timestamps transcends make: Ninja, CMake, Bazel, and every build system you touch in 2026 is a variation of it. Understand make and you understand the whole family.

make knows how to compile nothing: it knows how to compare dates and obey a graph. If the graph tells the truth, the incremental build is safe; if the graph lies, make lies along, with all the confidence in the world.

# From hand-written rule to pattern

Last lesson's Makefile repeats gcc -c three times and would repeat thirty in a real project. The evolution comes in three features. Variables: CC sets the compiler, CFLAGS the flags, OBJ the object list; switching -O2 to -Og becomes an edit in one place. Pattern rules: %.o: %.c teaches once how any .o is born from the matching .c. And the automatic variables inside recipes: $@ is the rule's target, $< is the first prerequisite, $^ is their complete list.

One syntax detail knocks beginners down to this day: the recipe line starts with a TAB, mandatorily. Spaces produce the cryptic missing separator, and every decent editor already knows this upon detecting a Makefile.

With this kit, the ten-file Makefile stays the size of the two-file one: one OBJ list, one link rule using $^ and $@, one pattern rule using $< to compile, and the -MMD -MP flags from the previous lesson handling headers via an include of the generated .d files.

CC      = gcc
CFLAGS  = -Wall -Wextra -O2 -MMD -MP
OBJ     = main.o mat.o es.o

all: app                 # first target = make's default

app: $(OBJ)
	$(CC) $^ -o $@       # $^ = all the .o files, $@ = app

%.o: %.c                 # pattern rule for any .o
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

clean:
	rm -f $(OBJ) $(OBJ:.o=.d) app

.PHONY: all clean        # targets that are not files
-include $(OBJ:.o=.d)    # generated header dependencies

## all, clean, and why .PHONY exists

Two targets became a universal convention. all is the default target, placed first so that a make with no arguments builds the whole project. clean erases the generated artifacts, objects, .d files, and the executable, returning the directory to pure-source state; it is the restart button when you suspect inconsistent builds.

.PHONY exists because of a real trap: to make, every target is in principle a FILE. If someone creates a file named clean in the directory, make looks, sees the clean file exists and has no newer prerequisites, and answers 'clean' is up to date without erasing anything. Declaring .PHONY: all clean warns that these targets correspond to no files and must execute whenever called.

Worth closing with honesty about the reach: for small and medium projects, a Makefile like this is concise and transparent, and you will find thousands of them in consecrated C libraries. When the project grows to multiple platforms, IDEs, and external dependencies, writing Makefiles by hand becomes suffering, and that is where the next lesson's CMake comes in.
A good Makefile reads in one screen: variables at the top, one pattern rule, all and clean marked .PHONY. If yours needs its own manual, it should have become CMake already.

# The generator that became the standard

CMake compiles nothing: it GENERATES the native build system, Makefiles on Linux, Ninja where you ask, IDE projects on Windows, from a portable description in CMakeLists.txt. This extra layer is what made it, in 2026, the C++ world's de facto standard: the same project builds on Linux with gcc, on Windows with MSVC, and on embedded with the ARM toolchain, rewriting nothing. IDEs like CLion, VS Code, and Visual Studio consume it natively, and the dependency ecosystem (vcpkg, Conan) speaks CMake as its mother tongue.

Modern CMake, from the post-3.0 era, revolves around TARGETS: each executable or library is an object with properties, its sources, its include directories, its flags, and dependencies are declared between targets, not in global variables scattered around.

The central command is target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE mat): it links mat into app and, together, propagates the usage properties mat declared as public. Includes and flags travel with the dependency, and the consumer needs to know nothing.

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(calc CXX)

add_library(mat src/mat.cpp)
target_include_directories(mat PUBLIC include)
target_compile_features(mat PUBLIC cxx_std_17)

add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE mat)

# Out-of-source: the whole build is born in build/
#   cmake -S . -B build
#   cmake --build build
# Sources untouched; deleting build/ is the perfect clean.

## PUBLIC, PRIVATE and the out-of-tree build

The modifiers are the model's heart. PRIVATE: the property holds only for compiling the target itself; an internal implementation detail. INTERFACE: holds only for whoever consumes the target; typical of header-only libraries. PUBLIC: holds for both sides. In the example, mat's include is PUBLIC because its headers appear both in the implementation and in the sources of whoever uses it; if it were an internal dependency, PRIVATE would spare consumers from inheriting what does not concern them. Declaring this right is what lets a large project compose without flag leakage.

The out-of-source build is the other discipline: generating everything in a separate build/ directory, never mixed with the sources. The gains are concrete: a clean git status, several configurations side by side (build-debug/, build-release/, build-arm/), and the most reliable clean there is, rm -rf build/.

The everyday flow boils down to two commands, cmake -S . -B build to configure and cmake --build build to compile, and it does not change whether the generator is Makefile, Ninja, or an IDE project.
Modern CMake is declaring targets and what each exposes, and letting propagation work. Whoever still scatters global flags is writing 2010's CMake with today's syntax.

# When the target is not your machine

Every build until here assumed a coincidence: the machine compiling is the one executing. It breaks all the time: an ARM microcontroller's firmware is compiled on your x86-64 desktop, because the chip would not even have memory to run gcc; the image for a MIPS router is born on a CI server; the app for a Raspberry Pi builds faster on your laptop. Compiling on one architecture to execute on another is cross-compilation, and it demands a special compiler: the cross-compiler, which RUNS on the host and GENERATES code for the target.

The target's name is encoded in the triplet, the tools' prefix: arm-none-eabi-gcc reads architecture arm, vendor none, ABI eabi, the classic kit for microcontrollers with no operating system (bare metal). Whereas aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc generates for 64-bit ARM with Linux and glibc. The triplet comes with the whole binutils: arm-none-eabi-as, arm-none-eabi-ld, arm-none-eabi-nm, the same roles you already know, speaking another machine.

The golden rule: a binary generated for the target does NOT run on the host; testing demands the hardware, an emulator like QEMU, or a lot of faith.

# toolchain-arm.cmake: the target profile for CMake
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME      Generic)   # bare metal, no OS
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR arm)
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER   arm-none-eabi-gcc)
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER arm-none-eabi-g++)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)

# Configure and compile without touching the project's CMakeLists:
#   cmake -S . -B build-arm \
#         -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=toolchain-arm.cmake
#   cmake --build build-arm
$ file build-arm/app.elf
app.elf: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, ARM, EABI5

## Sysroot: the piece of the target on your disk

Compiling for the target is not just generating its instructions: the code includes headers and links libraries, and they must be the TARGET's. Using your desktop's stdio.h to compile for an ARM Linux is a recipe for silent incompatibility. The answer is the sysroot: a directory on the host mirroring the target's system root, with its headers and its libraries, which the compiler consults via the --sysroot flag. Bare-metal toolchains like arm-none-eabi embed their own world, with newlib in place of glibc; toolchains for embedded Linux (Yocto, Buildroot) generate the sysroot along with the system image.

In CMake, all of this gets packaged in the example's toolchain file: a file saying who compiles, for which system, where to look for libraries, and instructing find_package to look in the sysroot, not on the host. The project stays the same; only the profile passed at configuration changes, and that is how the same CMakeLists generates build-x86/ and build-arm/ side by side.

Close with the sanity check: the file command on the artifact must state the TARGET's architecture. If it says x86-64, the toolchain file was not applied.

Cross-compiling is keeping two worlds separate in your head: the tools run on the host, but headers, libraries, and instructions belong to the target. Every pain in this area comes from mixing the two.

# Build time is people time

A twenty-minute build does not cost twenty minutes: it costs the focus of every person waiting, times the times a day they wait. That is the right ruler for deciding how much to invest here: team time saved versus the cost of the change. Two tools give a return disproportionate to the effort, and both plug into what you already have.

The first is ccache: a compilation cache. It positions itself in front of the compiler and, before calling gcc, computes the compilation's key, the preprocessed source, the flags, and the compiler version; if it has seen that key, it returns the stored object in milliseconds. The shining case is the restart: a make clean followed by a full build, or a branch switch and return, stops costing minutes because almost everything comes from the cache. On CI, with the cache persisted between jobs, the effect is dramatic.

The second is Ninja: a minimalist build executor, made to be GENERATED by tools like CMake, not written by hand. Nearly zero startup, well-used parallelism; the switch costs one -G Ninja at configuration.

# Ninja as CMake's generator:
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build          # ninja takes -j on its own

# ccache in front of the compiler via CMake:
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja \
      -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache

$ ccache -s                  # cache statistics
  cache hit (direct)     8241
  cache miss              913
  hit rate              90.0 %

# Cheap restart: rm -rf build, reconfigure, rebuild:
# almost everything comes back from cache in seconds.

## Reproducibility: same source, same binary

A reproducible build is one where the same source, with the same toolchain, produces identical bytes, on any machine and any date. It looks like a detail and is a foundation: it allows verifying that the distributed binary corresponds to the audited source, the basis of trust in software supply chains, and the Linux distributions invested heavily in it over the last decade.

The enemies are small and known: __DATE__ and __TIME__ macros stamping the build's time, absolute paths embedded in debug symbols, file order depending on the system. The weapons too: the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH variable freezes the date; -ffile-prefix-map remaps paths; and the rest is the discipline of pinning toolchain versions.

And there is the self-interested bonus: a deterministic build is a cacheable build. ccache lives on identical inputs producing identical outputs; every timestamp in the code is a hole in the cache. The module's final criterion: measure the team's build time, attack first what is cheap (parallelism, Ninja, ccache), and treat any source of nondeterminism as a bug, not a charm.
A slow build is a tax charged in human attention, and an irreproducible build is a debt of trust. Both bills are paid with the same coins: cache, determinism, and the courage to measure.

# The compiler warns; the amateur ignores

A warning is not decoration: it is the compiler saying your code compiles but smells like an error. And it is usually right. if (x = 5) instead of x == 5, comparing int with unsigned and getting a surreal result, returning without a value on one path of the function, using a variable before initializing: all of it is legal for the grammar and fatal for the logic, and all of it gcc denounces, as long as you ask.

The professional minimum request is -Wall -Wextra. Despite the name, -Wall does not turn on all warnings: it turns on the classic set of highest value; -Wextra adds another useful layer. The cost of typing the two flags is zero, and the return is an entire class of bugs dead before the first test runs.

The third pillar is -Werror: it promotes warnings to errors and breaks the build. It is what turns warning into CONTRACT: with -Werror on CI, no new warning enters the project, because the red build will not let it. Without it, warnings accumulate little by little until becoming noise of hundreds, and then nobody sees the new warning that mattered.

[["Warning","What it catches","Why it earns the ticket"],["-Wparentheses","assignment used as condition","the classic = instead of =="],["-Wuninitialized","reading a variable with no value","memory garbage becoming result"],["-Wsign-compare","comparison between signed and unsigned","loops that never end or never run"],["-Wunused-variable","variable declared and never used","refactoring leftovers and typos"],["-Wshadow","variable shadowing an outer one","the silent bug of the repeated name"]]

## How to adopt without suffering

On a new project, the recipe is dry: -Wall -Wextra -Werror from the first commit, and warnings simply never exist. On a legacy project with five hundred accumulated warnings, turning on -Werror at once stalls the team; the path is gradual: turn on -Wall -Wextra, zero the warnings module by module, and only then seal with -Werror against regression. CI tools help by marking the warning count as a metric that may only fall.

Two honesties to close. First: false positives exist, and the professional answer is not turning off the warning across the whole project, it is rewriting the stretch to become obvious (the = warning itself falls silent with intentional double parentheses) or suppressing pointwise with a justified pragma. Second: warnings depend on optimization; -Wmaybe-uninitialized, for instance, sees more with -O2, because flow analysis runs deeper. Running CI with the same flags as release is not pedantry, it is coverage.

The contract's summary: the compiler is the cheapest reviewer you have. It works for free, in milliseconds, on every build. It only needs you not to tell it to shut up.

A team living with five hundred warnings does not have five hundred problems: it has one, the habit of ignoring the free reviewer. The warning that matters tomorrow will be born invisible in the middle of the noise.

# Instrumenting to catch in the act

Warnings catch what can be proven without executing. A whole family of bugs, however, only reveals itself running: the access one byte past the array that TODAY crashes nothing, the use-after-free corrupting silently, the signed overflow module 3 showed becoming the optimizer's license. For those there are sanitizers, present in GCC and Clang: the compiler INSTRUMENTS the binary, inserting checks around every suspicious access, and the program starts denouncing itself at the exact moment of the crime, with a stack trace pointing at the culprit.

AddressSanitizer, ASan (-fsanitize=address), covers memory errors: buffer overflow on the heap, stack, and globals, use-after-free, double free, and leaks via the embedded LeakSanitizer. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, UBSan (-fsanitize=undefined), catches UB in the act: signed overflow, invalid shift, null dereference, division by zero. ThreadSanitizer, TSan (-fsanitize=thread), hunts data races: two concurrent accesses without synchronization, the bug that vanishes when you try to reproduce it.

The magic has a price, and the next section says where to pay it.

int main(void) {
    int v[10];
    return v[10];            // one past the end: classic UB
}

$ gcc -g -fsanitize=address estouro.c && ./a.out
==5231==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow
READ of size 4 at 0x7ffd63d2a3d8
    #0 0x55e1c1 in main estouro.c:3
Address ... is located in stack of thread T0 at offset
40 in frame ... 'v' <== the report itself names the array

# UBSan on signed overflow:
$ gcc -g -fsanitize=undefined soma.c && ./a.out
soma.c:2:14: runtime error: signed integer overflow:
2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'

[["Sanitizer","Flag","What it catches","Typical runtime cost"],["ASan","-fsanitize=address","overflows, use-after-free, leaks","around 2x slower"],["UBSan","-fsanitize=undefined","signed overflow, null, invalid shift","light, often negligible"],["TSan","-fsanitize=thread","data races between threads","5x to 15x, and more memory"],["ASan + UBSan","combined flags","the standard testing pair","dominated by ASan's cost"]]

## Where to run: tests yes, production almost never

The cost defines the place. ASan around 2x time and multiplied memory; UBSan light; TSan heavy, 5x to 15x, and incompatible with ASan in the same binary, so it runs on a separate build. None of it belongs in the production binary; all of it belongs in the TESTS. The consecrated practice in 2026: the test suite runs on CI in two instrumented variants, one with ASan and UBSan together, another with TSan for threaded code, besides the normal build. Every test execution becomes a free memory and UB sweep.

Three usage tips that save afternoons: compile with -g so the stack trace cites file and line; combine with -fno-omit-frame-pointer for more faithful traces; and treat ANY report as a real bug, because a sanitizer practically gives no false positive: it saw the illegal access happen.

And connect it with module 3: UBSan is the practical answer to the UB chapter. Where the optimizer assumes overflow does not exist, UBSan proves otherwise with address and line. Fuzzing and instrumented production are refinements that exist, but the habit that changes the game is one: tests always pass clean under sanitizer.
The sanitizer turns the memory bug from ghost into flagrante: instead of corrupting quietly and exploding far away, the program stops on the crime's line with the signed confession.

# The reviewer that reads everything

Between the compiler's warning and the sanitizer's flagrante there is a third layer: dedicated static analysis, which examines the code WITHOUT executing it, following paths, possible values, and API contracts with more depth than normal compilation allows itself. The reference tool in the 2026 C++ ecosystem is clang-tidy, built on Clang's front end, with hundreds of checks organized in families: bugprone- for error-prone patterns, modernize- for suggesting modern C++, performance- for unnecessary copies and allocations, readability- for clarity.

The difference from the sanitizer is structural, not of quality: the sanitizer needs the bug to HAPPEN in a test to catch it; the static analyzer sees the dangerous path even if no test passes through it. In exchange, without executing, it sometimes accuses paths impossible in practice: false positives exist and are part of the deal.

Beyond clang-tidy, the market uses cppcheck, the compilers' own analyzers (gcc -fanalyzer) and commercial platforms; the choosing criterion is integration into your flow, not ranking.

std::string& primeiro(std::vector<std::string>& v) {
    std::string s = v[0];
    return s;                 // reference to a dead local
}

$ clang-tidy lista.cpp -- -std=c++17
lista.cpp:3:12: warning: reference to stack memory
associated with local variable 's' returned
[clang-diagnostic-return-stack-address]

# No test ran; the dangerous path was READ.
# Typical integration: clang-tidy uses compile_commands.json
$ cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON

[["Layer","When it acts","Needs to execute?","False positive"],["Warnings (-Wall -Wextra)","on every compilation","no","rare"],["Static analysis (clang-tidy)","on demand and on CI","no","exists, demands triage"],["Sanitizers (ASan, UBSan)","running the tests","yes","practically zero"],["Debugger (gdb)","directed investigation","yes","not applicable"]]

## Integrating without becoming noise

An analysis tool nobody runs does not exist. Mature integration has three steps. First, clang-tidy needs to know HOW each file is compiled, flags and includes; that comes from compile_commands.json, which CMake exports with one flag and Ninja itself feeds. Second, the configuration lives in a .clang-tidy file versioned at the repository root: the team picks the enabled check families, and the choice holds for everyone, in the editor and on CI. Third, the trigger: in the editor via clangd, which underlines the problem as you type, and on CI running over the files changed in the pull request, not over the whole repository on every build.

The biggest adoption mistake is turning everything on on day one: hundreds of checks over a legacy generate thousands of findings, the team drowns and turns the tool off forever. The path that works: start with bugprone- and the correctness checks, zero them, and expand family by family, with the same gradual logic as -Werror.

Like the warning, the analyzer's finding is a conversation, not a verdict: read it, understand the scenario it describes, and only then fix or suppress with justification in the code.
The sanitizer needs the bug to happen; the static analyzer only needs it to be possible. One catches it in the test that passed over it; the other reads the path no test has visited yet.

# Stopping time inside the process

The hour comes when printf is not enough: you need to stop the program mid-flight and look inside. gdb does exactly that, and the essentials fit in six commands. Compile with -g (and preferably -Og, as module 3 taught) and open with gdb ./app. break main.c:42, abbreviated b, plants a breakpoint; run, or r, executes until it. Stopped, next (n) executes the line and steps OVER function calls; step (s) enters them. print total (p) shows the value of any expression in scope; continue (c) releases the program until the next breakpoint.

The sixth command is what solves crashes: backtrace, or bt, prints the whole call stack, from where the program is down to main, with file and line of each frame. On a segmentation fault, gdb stops by itself at the crash point, and bt answers the question that matters: how did the program GET here? The frame, up, and down commands navigate between frames so you inspect each level's variables.

With these six, you cover most real debugging sessions.

## Core dump: debugging the death after it

Not every crash happens in front of you. The program fell at dawn, on the server, on the client's machine; running again under gdb may not even reproduce it. For that there is the core dump: the system photographs the process's memory at the instant of death, and gdb opens that photo afterwards, the so-called post-mortem. You cannot step with next, the process is gone, but you can do everything that is reading: backtrace, inspect each frame's variables, understand the exact state of the disaster.

In modern practice, on systemd distributions, coredumpctl lists recent dumps and coredumpctl gdb opens the latest straight in the debugger. In the classic scheme, the core file appears in the process's directory, provided the limit is open: ulimit -c unlimited is the session's switch. Two requirements for the session to pay off: the binary with -g (or the corresponding symbol packages in production) and the EXACT binary that generated the dump, otherwise the addresses match nothing.

Tie the module's ends together: the sanitizer catches the corruption in tests; the core dump tells what happened when it escaped to production. The two tools tell the same story at different times.

# The discussion that does not deserve humans

Braces on the same line or the next? Spaces or tabs? Eighty columns or a hundred and twenty? Teams have burned weeks on these wars, and the professional answer in 2026 is admitting the discussion does not deserve people: choose ONCE, write the choice in a file, and let a machine apply it forever. In the C and C++ world, the machine is clang-format, clang-tidy's sibling in the LLVM family.

The contract is simple: a .clang-format file at the repository root, versioned with the code, describes the style: base style (LLVM, Google, among others), line width, brace policy, include sorting. Anyone runs clang-format -i and the file is rewritten to standard; the editor does it on save, with nobody thinking about it.

Notice what this is NOT: clang-format does not judge names, does not detect bugs, does not opine on architecture; it only positions text. That is deliberate: formatting is the only layer where automation can be total, because there is no case where the answer depends on business context.

# .clang-format at the repository root
BasedOnStyle: LLVM
IndentWidth: 4
ColumnLimit: 100
BreakBeforeBraces: Attach
SortIncludes: CaseSensitive

# Format a file in place:
clang-format -i src/caixa.cpp

# CI: fail if something escaped the standard (without rewriting):
clang-format --dry-run --Werror src/*.cpp

# Pre-commit: format only what is going into the commit
git diff --name-only --cached | grep -E "\.(c|h|cpp|hpp)$" \
  | xargs clang-format -i

## The most valuable side effect: the code review

The gain that justifies everything is not aesthetic, it is social: formatting leaves the code review. Without a formatter, every pull request becomes a hunt for spaces and commas: comments about indentation bury the questions that mattered, and the author leaves the review having defended braces instead of having discussed the design. With format guaranteed by machine, the diff shows only LOGIC change, and the reviewer spends attention where it pays: names, edge cases, architecture.

Adoption on a legacy has one specific trap: formatting the whole repository at once creates a giant commit polluting git blame. The usual ways out: doing that formatting in an isolated commit and listing it in .git-blame-ignore-revs, which git knows how to skip; or formatting file by file, as they get touched. Choose with the team, document, follow.

And a coexistence rule that avoids friction: the chosen style does not need to be your favorite, it needs to be the TEAM's. Consistency is worth more than any individual preference; after a week, nobody sees the style anymore, and that is exactly the victory.
Every minute of code review spent on indentation is a minute stolen from a question about design. Formatting is a solved problem: hand it to the machine and never give it back to humans.
