# The lab in three files

This module is a workbench: you will take a minimal program and walk it through everything the trail taught, phase by phase, with your own hands. The program is a statistics calculator: mat.h declares two functions, media and maior; mat.cpp defines them; main.cpp uses them on a fixed vector and prints the result. Three files, two translation units, one boundary header: the smallest scenario where the whole toolchain appears.

The route mirrors the previous modules. In this lesson, we assemble the files and check the map of what will happen. In lesson 2, we compile each unit separately with -c and read the objects with nm, finding the undefined symbol theory promised. In lesson 3, we link, break the link on purpose to watch undefined reference be born and die, and package mat into a static library. In lesson 4, we compare O0 and O2 in the assembly, measure with -Os, and close with strip.

Reproduce every command on a Linux with g++ installed. Reading is good; typing and seeing with your own eyes is what sticks.

## The map of what will happen

Before running any command, predict with theory. The preprocessor will paste mat.h inside each .cpp: main.cpp learns that media and maior EXIST without seeing the bodies, exactly module 1's tunnel vision. The compiler accepts the calls trusting the declarations; the assembler records in main.o the calls with open addresses and the corresponding relocation entries.

Predict the nm: main.o will have T for main and U for media, maior, and printf, all decorated by the C++ mangling module 4 introduced; mat.o will have T for media and maior, and no U beyond what the implementation needs. The link will join the two, pay the relocations, and printf will remain U in the executable, promised to the dynamic libc at load time, the dynamic linking topic of module 1.

If every sentence of this map sounded natural, the trail fulfilled the theoretical half. The other half is watching the map become reality in the terminal, and that is where we go now.
An engineer predicting the output before running the command is not guessing: they are testing their own mental model. The terminal only confirms or corrects; whoever learns is the prediction.

# Two units, two objects

Hands on the terminal. g++ -c main.cpp and g++ -c mat.cpp produce main.o and mat.o: two independent compilations, as in a large project they would run in parallel. Notice main.cpp compiled clean even with NO body of media nearby: the declaration's promise sufficed, as predicted on the map.

Now the magnifying glass. nm main.o lists the decorated symbols: _Z5mediaPKii and _Z5maiorPKii with U, printf with U, main with T. The strange names are module 4's mangling encoding the parameters (PKi is pointer to const int); nm -C main.o translates back to media(int const*, int) and company. On the other side, nm -C mat.o shows the two functions with T: defined, with an address inside the object.

This is module 1's half-signed contract, now visible: main.o consumes what mat.o provides. Neither runs alone; main.o has calls pointing at emptiness, awaiting relocation. Save both nm outputs; in the next lesson, the linker settles the accounts, and comparing before and after is worth it.

$ g++ -c main.cpp && g++ -c mat.cpp
$ ls
main.cpp  main.o  mat.cpp  mat.h  mat.o

$ nm main.o
0000000000000000 T main
                 U printf
                 U _Z5maiorPKii
                 U _Z5mediaPKii

$ nm -C mat.o
0000000000000000 T maior(int const*, int)
0000000000000024 T media(int const*, int)

$ echo _Z5mediaPKii | c++filt
media(int const*, int)

[["Command","What it showed","Trail concept in action"],["g++ -c main.cpp","compiled with no body of media at all","a declaration suffices for the unit to close"],["nm main.o","decorated U's and main's T","undefined symbols are promises"],["nm -C mat.o","media and maior with T","definitions with an address in the object"],["c++filt","_Z5mediaPKii becomes media(int const*, int)","mangling encodes the signature"]]

## The experiment: creating a U on purpose

To feel the mechanism, provoke it. Add to main.cpp a call to a function that does NOT exist anywhere: declare double desvio(const int* v, int n); right after the include and call desvio(notas, 5) inside the printf. Recompile only main: g++ -c main.cpp. It compiles clean, again, because a declaration suffices. And nm now shows a third decorated U: _Z6desvioPKii, a promise NOBODY in the project fulfills.

This object is perfectly healthy in the compiler's eyes and fatally ill in the linker's, and that is the lesson: -c pushes the charge forward. On real teams that is how builds break at the end: every file compiles, the link blows up, and someone who does not know the phases loses an hour looking for the error in the wrong place.

Leave desvio there on purpose: the next lesson links this project, watches the famous error be born with decorated name and all, and fixes it in two rounds. Breaking on purpose is the cheapest way to learn to fix.
-c compiles every promise without checking whether anyone fulfills it; nm is the list of promises. Whoever reads the list before the link is never surprised by the collector.

# The famous error, now on purpose

Time to link with the bomb armed from the previous lesson: g++ main.o mat.o -o calc. ld answers on the spot: undefined reference to 'desvio(int const*, int)', with collect2 closing the parade. Read calmly the anatomy studied in module 4: the linker speaks, the symbol comes demangled in modern g++'s message, and the cause is the list of promises with no fulfiller. Run the method: nm -C main.o | grep desvio confirms the U; no other object has the T. Diagnosis closed in seconds, because you KNEW where to look.

Fix one: remove the desvio call and declaration, recompile main.cpp, link again. Green build, ./calc prints media 81.0 maior 100. Fix two, more interesting: define desvio in mat.cpp (and declare it in mat.h), living the real routine of evolving the boundary between units.

Now the second classic experiment: forgetting an object. g++ main.o -o calc, without mat.o, brings the link down with TWO undefined references, media and maior. The same error, another cause from module 4's list: the provider stayed out of the command.

$ g++ main.o mat.o -o calc
/usr/bin/ld: main.o: in function 'main':
main.cpp:(.text+0x2f): undefined reference to
                       'desvio(int const*, int)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

$ g++ main.o -o calc          # forgetting mat.o on purpose
/usr/bin/ld: main.o: undefined reference to
                     'media(int const*, int)'
/usr/bin/ld: main.o: undefined reference to
                     'maior(int const*, int)'

# With the source fixed and both objects:
$ g++ main.o mat.o -o calc && ./calc
media 81.0 maior 100

## Packaging into a static library

The lesson's last step: turning mat into a real library. ar rcs libmat.a mat.o creates the package; the link becomes g++ main.o -L. -lmat -o calc. It works identically, and now you can reenact module 4's order lesson at home: g++ -lmat main.o -L. -o calc breaks on many toolchain versions, because the library was examined before any pending existed. If on your Linux that command passes, you bumped into behavior variations between versions and distributions, and it is worth investigating which ld is in use; the principle of putting whoever uses before whoever provides remains the only guaranteed arrangement.

Close the lesson with ldd on the executable: it lists libc and the dynamic loader, the dependencies left for load time, while your libmat.a was already copied into the binary, invisible to ldd. Static inside, dynamic outside: module 1's dichotomy, now in YOUR binary.

The full cycle happened in your hands: break, read, diagnose with nm, fix by two paths, package. That muscle is what the final lesson consolidates.
Provoking the undefined reference on purpose is vaccination: the first time hurts in a controlled environment, and all the later ones, in real work, become thirty-second diagnoses.

# O0 and O2 side by side, on your code

Second-to-last station: watching the optimizer work on YOUR project. Generate mat's two assemblies: g++ -S -O0 mat.cpp -o mat_O0.s and g++ -S -O2 mat.cpp -o mat_O2.s. Open both (or paste media into godbolt, as in module 3) and apply the essential reading: at -O0, the function loads and stores variables on the stack at every step, with [rbp-...] accesses everywhere and the loop faithfully bureaucratic. At -O2, the stack accesses vanish, the sum lives in a register, and depending on the GCC version the loop appears vectorized, processing blocks of elements with xmm registers.

Do the second comparison, now of size: compile the whole project three times, with -O0, -O2, and -Os, and run size on each executable. On a program this small the differences are modest, and that is exactly the honest learning: -Os's dramatic gains appear when there is a LOT of code to slim; here you observe the mechanism with small, true numbers.

Write down the three .text numbers: they are your first binary engineering measurement.

$ g++ -S -O0 mat.cpp -o mat_O0.s
$ g++ -S -O2 mat.cpp -o mat_O2.s
$ wc -l mat_O0.s mat_O2.s
  118 mat_O0.s
   74 mat_O2.s     # fewer lines, and no stack accesses

$ g++ -O2 main.cpp mat.cpp -o calc
$ size calc
   text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
   2103     640       8    2751     abf calc

$ g++ -O2 -g main.cpp mat.cpp -o calc && ls -lh calc
-rwxrwxr-x 1 dev dev 27K calc      # with debug symbols
$ strip calc && ls -lh calc
-rwxrwxr-x 1 dev dev 15K calc      # only what is needed to run

## strip: the final cut

Close the cycle with the delivery build: g++ -O2 -g main.cpp mat.cpp -o calc, size to record the sections, ls -lh to see the file with debug symbols, and then strip calc. The executable plummets in size without changing a byte of executable code: gdb's luggage left, as in module 4. Run ./calc one last time to confirm nothing functional was lost.

It is worth making explicit the professional flow this gesture summarizes: you compile WITH -g always, because debug symbols cost no performance; you distribute the binary stripped; and you keep the version with symbols (or a separate symbol file) to open production core dumps, module 6's post-mortem. Throwing the symbols away without keeping a copy is saving cents today to pay dearly on the first night of crashes.

The project ends here on the technical side: you compiled separately, read objects, broke and fixed the link, packaged a library, compared optimizations, and slimmed the final artifact. The last lesson adds no commands; it organizes what these four left in your hand.
Measure first, cut later, always confirm: size, strip, and a final ./calc. Optimization without measurement is faith; with measurement, it becomes engineering, even when the numbers are small.

# What changed between the first gcc and this one

At this trail's start, gcc ola.c -o ola was a spell: text went in, an executable came out, and any error in between was an irritating mystery. Look at what that same command means to you now: a preprocessor pasting headers, a compiler walking through lexer, parser, semantic analysis, and an optimized intermediate representation, an assembler generating objects full of promises, and a linker closing each one into a measurable binary. The black box became a glass box: the gears are still complex, but you SEE them.

Take inventory of what stayed in your hand. You read errors by the phase that emitted them and fix the first, not the fortieth. You open objects with nm and executables with ldd before theorizing. You treat undefined reference as a thirty-second diagnosis. You choose optimization level with criteria and check on godbolt what the compiler did. You declare builds in make or CMake understanding the graph underneath. And you surround your own code with warnings, sanitizers, static analysis, gdb, and automatic formatting.

None of these gestures is decorative: each was born from a real problem you watched happen.

[["Work situation","The reflex the trail installed"],["confusing build error","identify the phase by the message and attack the first error"],["missing symbol at link","nm on both sides: who consumes, who should provide"],["performance doubt","look at the assembly on godbolt before opining"],["intermittent memory bug","run the suite under ASan and UBSan and read the flagrante"],["slow or fragile build","check the dependency graph, cache, and parallelism"],["production crash","core dump opened in gdb with the symbols kept"]]
A respected tool is an understood tool: whoever knows what the toolchain does underneath stops fighting it and starts using it as an ally.

## The habit that stays

If a single habit summarizes everything, it is this: looking under the hood as routine, not as heroism. It costs seconds: an nm after compiling, a size after linking, a peek at godbolt before discussing performance, a -Wall -Wextra on every new project you create. Each of these peeks confirms or corrects your mental model, and it is the sharpened mental model that turns hours of trial and error into minutes of diagnosis.

Keep practicing with what really exists out there: recompile an open-source library watching its build, read the Makefile or CMakeLists of a project you admire, open a binary on your system with nm and ldd just to check what you recognize. This trail's material remains available for revisiting, and the tools, gcc, clang, nm, make, cmake, gdb and company, are installed or one command away on any Linux.

The box is open and lit. Keep the flashlight on: it is light, and what it shows is worth every second of the looking.
